prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that you referred to soccer as 'football' in a public establishment. Respond to the committee.
response:
Mr. Chairman, distinguished members of the Cookout Division,

I appear before you today not to evade, but to clarify. I understand the gravity of this allegation. To refer to soccer as “football” in a public establishment is, on its face, a linguistic provocation. It suggests a sympathy with foreign nomenclature that runs counter to the established American tradition of gridiron, hot dogs, and the sacred Fourth Down.

However, I must respectfully submit that my words were not an act of subversion, but one of historical context.

The term “football,” as I used it, was not a rejection of American values, but an acknowledgment of etymological roots. The sport derives its name from the fact that it is played *on foot*, as opposed to on horseback—a distinction dating back to medieval Europe, long before the forward pass or the two-minute warning were conceived. My usage was pedantic, Mr. Chairman, not political. It was the utterance of a man who has read too many rulebooks, not one who seeks to undermine the cultural sovereignty of the American backyard barbecue.

Furthermore, I would remind this committee that the Cookout itself is a melting pot. We grill bratwursts of German origin, serve kimchi alongside coleslaw, and enjoy music born from a fusion of global traditions. If our plates can accommodate diversity without surrendering their essential American character, surely our vocabulary can withstand a single, historically accurate synonym without collapsing into un-American chaos.

I have never refused to call the NFL “football.” I have never disparaged the pigskin. I have merely recognized that language, like a good marinade, is enriched by its many ingredients.

If acknowledging the linguistic ancestry of a sport makes me suspect, then I stand guilty of curiosity. But if this committee seeks true loyalty to the American cookout, I pledge that my devotion to charred meat, cold beverages, and communal fellowship remains unshaken—regardless of what one calls the game being watched on the patio television.

I yield the remainder of my time, and humbly request that the committee consider the spirit in which the word was spoken, rather than the syllables alone.
